newsitem.title: SURINAM: Surinam's president makes transition to democracy.
newsitem.headline: Surinam's president makes transition to democracy.

text.p: Surinam's new president Jules Wijdenbosch on Thursday became the first member of the former military government to be democratically chosen to lead the South American country.

Wijdenbosch, 55, who is backed by former military strongman Desi Bouterse, defeated previous President Ronald Venetiaan in the closest presidential run-off since Surinam won independence from the Netherlands in 1975.
He is expected to be sworn in on Sept. 14 for a five-year term.
The secret ballot of more than 800 national and regional politicians reversed a 1991 vote in which Venetiaan easily defeated Wijdenbosch.
Wijdenbosch's victory brought Bouterse's National Democratic Party its first election success in three attempts.
The former civil servant who studied politics at the University of Amsterdam was a founding member of the NDP.
A close friend of Bouterse, who staged two coups and ruled the former Dutch colony during the 1980s, Wijdenbosch held several key cabinet posts in the governments of the military regime.

Bouterse named Wijdenbosch vice-president and finance minister in the interim government installed after the so-called telephone coup on Christmas eve 1990 when military leaders rang government officials to tell them the government has been overthrown.
During this period Wijdenbosch became famous for very lax fiscal policy as the government spent heavily on populist measures in an effort to garner support ahead of the 1991 elections.
By the time Venetiaan became president, Wijdenbosch's policies had run down the central bank's reserves to zero and left the Surinamese guilder grossly overvalued.

Wijdenbosch, regarded by political analysts as more politically astute than charismatic, ran on a vague platform in the 1996 elections that focused on the recessive effects of the government's economic adjustment programme.
Before Thursday's vote he had said that if elected he would consult with leaders from all sectors of society to draw up political and economic policies.
Wijdenbosch had appeared to stand little chance of becoming president after the NDP was defeated by Venetiaan's New Front coalition in national elections in May.
But in the months that followed Bouterse and Wijdenbosch managed to persuade many New Front members to defect, leaving Venetiaan's coalition in tatters.
